blocks.text: 1. What Is RAG

blocks.alt: A query goes through retrieval, then generation, to produce a response

blocks.text: Agentic AI closed out the Deep Learning course by exploring models that take actions. RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, connects a language model to an external, searchable knowledge source, and opens a focused, dedicated course of its own.
This topic opens the RAG and Vector Search fundamentals that every other topic in this course builds on.
2. Recapping Generation Alone
A plain language model, relying on next token prediction, only draws on knowledge frozen inside its own trained weights.
RAG adds a second, live source of information the model can draw on when generating an answer.
3. The Two Stage Structure

blocks.alt: A retrieval stage feeds a generation stage

blocks.text: RAG splits every answer into two distinct stages: retrieval, then generation.
Retrieval finds relevant text, and generation writes the actual answer using it. That two-stage split is what defines RAG as an architecture.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Stage","What it does"],"rows":[["Retrieval","Finds relevant passages from an external source"],["Generation","Writes an answer using those retrieved passages"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Retrieval Stage Preview
The retrieval stage searches a document collection for the most relevant passages.
It does this by comparing a query against stored embeddings using cosine similarity, the same mechanism covered in Sentence Embeddings.
5. Generation Stage Preview

blocks.alt: Retrieved documents go through an LLM to produce an answer

blocks.text: The generation stage then feeds those retrieved passages into the model's prompt.
Building on the prompting techniques covered earlier, this lets the model answer using that fresh, retrieved context rather than relying on memory alone.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This two-stage handoff explains why RAG needs both a strong retrieval system and a strong language model working together, not either one alone.

blocks.text: 6. Why RAG Rather Than Just Asking The Model

blocks.alt: An LLM alone is compared against an LLM with RAG

blocks.text: Asking a plain model directly only surfaces whatever it happened to memorize during training.
RAG lets that same model answer using current, specific, or private information instead, which is its real practical advantage.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question type","Best answered by"],"rows":[["General, stable knowledge","A plain language model alone"],["Current, specific, or private information","RAG, retrieving fresh context first"]]}

blocks.text: 7. RAG As An Architecture Pattern

blocks.alt: RAG is a pattern, not one fixed tool

blocks.text: RAG is not one single algorithm. It is an architecture pattern combining several components.
Each of those component pieces is covered in its own dedicated depth in the topics ahead.
8. Recognizing Why RAG Matters As This Course's Own Starting Point

blocks.alt: Needing grounded, up-to-date answers points toward using RAG

blocks.text: RAG grounds answers in real, external, current information.
For a stable, general knowledge task, the kind covered under Transfer Learning, a plain language model alone remains sufficient.
9. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates the two stage RAG structure by retrieving a passage and using it to construct a grounded prompt.

code.content:
document_collection = [
    "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 in Paris.",
    "The Great Wall of China is over 13000 miles long.",
    "Mount Everest is the tallest mountain above sea level.",
]

def simple_retrieve(query, documents):
    # the retrieval stage: score each document by word overlap with the query
    query_words = set(query.lower().split())
    scored = []
    for doc in documents:
        overlap = len(query_words & set(doc.lower().split()))
        scored.append((doc, overlap))
    scored.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return scored[0][0]

def build_grounded_prompt(query, retrieved_passage):
    # the generation stage: build a prompt containing the retrieved context
    return f"Context: {retrieved_passage}\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer:"

query = "When was the Eiffel Tower completed?"
retrieved = simple_retrieve(query, document_collection)
print(f"Query: {query}")
print(f"Retrieved passage: {retrieved}")

grounded_prompt = build_grounded_prompt(query, retrieved)
print(f"\nGrounded prompt sent to the language model:\n{grounded_prompt}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows one relevant passage retrieved from a small document collection and inserted directly into a prompt before generation, matching the two-stage structure described above.

blocks.text: 10. Common Mistakes

items: Treating RAG as a single algorithm rather than an architecture combining retrieval and generation.
Assuming a plain language model can answer questions about current or private information on its own.
Skipping the retrieval stage entirely and hoping the model already knows the answer.
Forgetting that generation quality depends heavily on how relevant the retrieved passages actually are.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: RAG connects a language model to an external, searchable knowledge source.
A plain language model only draws on knowledge frozen inside its own trained weights.
RAG splits every answer into two stages: retrieval, then generation.
Retrieval searches a document collection for the most relevant passages using embeddings.
Generation feeds those retrieved passages into the model's prompt to produce the actual answer.
RAG lets a model answer using current, specific, or private information, not just memorized knowledge.
RAG is an architecture pattern combining several components, each explored in depth in this course.
Next up: Why RAG Is Needed, exploring the specific problems this architecture actually solves.
